method: Collected by hand for the prototype on 14 Oct 2026 from the publicly available part of each article. Every story uses the same format: what happened, who's involved, background, why it happened, what's next.

items.title: Airbus net orders pass 1,100 at nine-month mark
items.author: David Kaminski-Morrow
items.summary: Airbus's net orders for 2026 passed 1,100 aircraft by the end of September, even though the month itself was quiet, with just two new deals for A320neo-family jets.

brief.what: Airbus's net orders for 2026 passed 1,100 aircraft by the end of September. September itself was quiet, with only two new orders.
brief.who: Airbus; Air Cairo (15 A320neos); FlyOne Armenia (two A321neos); an unnamed customer that cancelled three A220-300s.
brief.context: Net orders are new orders minus cancellations, so they show real demand building in the backlog. Airbus is targeting 870 deliveries this year.
brief.why: Steady demand for the A320neo family carried the year-to-date total, even in a slow month.
brief.next: The full-year order and delivery tallies come in January; deliveries against the 870 target are the number to watch.

items.title: Inside Chromalloy's push to disrupt engine OEMs' aftermarket stranglehold
items.author: Jon Hemmerdinger
items.summary: Turbofan parts maker Chromalloy is expanding to challenge engine OEMs in the lucrative aftermarket, while also selling into demand from AI data centres.

brief.what: Chromalloy, a maker of turbofan engine parts, is expanding to compete with engine manufacturers for aftermarket repair and parts work, and to supply AI data centres.
brief.who: Chromalloy; the big engine makers (OEMs) that dominate the aftermarket.
brief.context: Engine makers earn much of their profit from parts and repairs after the sale. Chromalloy's new site in Oldsmar, Florida runs a $30 million ceramic-coating machine and could double output to 100,000 parts a year.
brief.why: Demand is growing in both markets at once; FlightGlobal frames it as a push to loosen engine makers' grip on aftermarket work.
brief.next: The public report doesn't say.

items.title: Joby faces $116.9m in damages for trade-secret misappropriation and NDA breach
items.author: Brooke Ingemi
items.summary: A Florida federal jury found the air taxi developer breached an NDA with supplier Aerosonic and misused its trade secrets. Joby denies wrongdoing.

brief.what: A federal jury in Florida found air taxi developer Joby Aero breached a nondisclosure agreement and misused a supplier's trade secrets, awarding $116.9 million in damages.
brief.who: Joby Aero (eVTOL developer, defendant); Aerosonic (sensor supplier, plaintiff).
brief.context: Aerosonic supplied Joby with 10 air-data probes for its eVTOL aircraft under a mutual NDA.
brief.why: The jury found Joby used Aerosonic's confidential information improperly. Joby denies all wrongdoing.
brief.next: Joby says it will "vigorously pursue" post-trial remedies, so the case isn't over.

items.title: ZeroAvia targets early 2027 to close critical Series D funding
items.author: Dominic Perry
items.summary: The hydrogen-electric engine start-up needs new money by mid-2027 or faces more cutbacks, with UK losses above £110 million.

brief.what: Hydrogen-electric engine start-up ZeroAvia needs new funding by the second quarter of 2027 or faces more cutbacks, and aims to close a Series D round in early 2027.
brief.who: ZeroAvia and its UK operation; future investors in the Series D round.
brief.context: Cumulative losses at the UK unit are above £110 million. ZeroAvia has flight-tested its ZA600 system on a modified Dornier 228.
brief.why: Its UK accounts show losses building up (over £110 million) while the technology is still in development, so it depends on new investment.
brief.next: Whether the Series D closes on time. The round's size and investors haven't been disclosed.

items.title: Biman Bangladesh orders its first Airbus jets: four A350s and six A321neos
items.author: Airbus press release
items.summary: The all-Boeing flag carrier placed a firm order for 10 Airbus aircraft to support planned routes to North America, Europe and the Middle East.

brief.what: Biman Bangladesh Airlines placed a firm order for 10 Airbus jets: four A350-900 widebodies and six A321neo narrowbodies.
brief.who: Biman Bangladesh (the national airline, previously all-Boeing); Airbus; Biman chairman Rumee A. Hossain.
brief.context: It is Biman's first Airbus order. Airbus claims the A350 burns about 25% less fuel than previous-generation rivals and the A321neo at least 20% less (manufacturer figures).
brief.why: Biman wants to expand internationally, including new routes to North America, Europe and the Middle East. Hossain cited Bangladesh's growing population, large diaspora and trade.
brief.next: Delivery dates weren't given in the announcement.

also.title: Boeing operator Biman Bangladesh opts to order Airbus jets

items.title: FAA approves JetBlue's $58.5m purchase of Spirit's LaGuardia slots
items.author: Helwing Villamizar
items.summary: JetBlue gets 22 former Spirit slots at slot-constrained LaGuardia after outbidding Frontier by $1 million at the bankruptcy auction.

brief.what: The FAA gave final approval for JetBlue to buy 22 former Spirit Airlines slots at New York's LaGuardia airport for $58.5 million.
brief.who: JetBlue (buyer); Spirit Airlines (bankrupt seller); Frontier (losing bidder at $57.5m); the FAA; the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey.
brief.context: Spirit stopped flying on 2 May 2026. LaGuardia is slot-controlled, so the right to take off and land there is scarce and valuable.
brief.why: The FAA said keeping the slots with a low-fare airline helps passengers and competition; JetBlue will hold under 5% of LaGuardia's slots.
brief.next: JetBlue can't sell or lease the slots before April 2028 and is evaluating up to 12 more daily LaGuardia round trips in 2027.

also.title: JetBlue's Purchase Of Spirit's LaGuardia Slots Gets FAA Approval

items.title: At least 81 US aircraft worth up to $3.3bn lost or damaged in Iran war
items.author: Ahmed Diab
items.summary: A CBO report puts US military aircraft losses in the Iran campaign at $1.9bn to $3.3bn, most of them MQ-9 Reaper drones.

brief.what: The Congressional Budget Office says at least 81 US military aircraft have been lost or damaged in the war with Iran, at a cost of $1.9 billion to $3.3 billion.
brief.who: The CBO; the Pentagon; 45 Senate Democrats and one independent who asked for a cost breakdown; Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
brief.context: The losses include 12 F-15Es, one F-35A, seven KC-135 tankers and 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones. The CBO estimates the whole war has cost about $38 billion, rising roughly $2 billion a month.
brief.why: The campaign, which began on 28 February, has no lasting ceasefire. Analyst Harlan Ullman notes that cheap drones can inflict heavy damage on large militaries.
brief.next: Senators want a detailed breakdown; the Pentagon says it has "nothing further to provide".

items.title: Brazil's regulator clears American Airlines' 8% stake in Azul, with conditions
items.author: John Huston
items.summary: CADE approved American's $100 million investment in Azul, provided the airlines sign an enforceable agreement limiting information sharing.

brief.what: Brazil's competition regulator CADE conditionally approved American Airlines' $100 million investment for about 8% of Azul.
brief.who: American Airlines; Azul; CADE; United (which already raised its Azul stake to about 8%); Abra Group, owner of rival GOL.
brief.context: Azul emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2026, with US carriers taking minority stakes.
brief.why: CADE was concerned about information sharing and coordination on Brazil-US routes, so it required an enforceable Merger Control Agreement.
brief.next: Abra Group has appealed an earlier approval, according to Reuters; the outcome is open.

items.title: Economics Nobel goes to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for work on stabilising economies
items.author: Philip Ball
items.summary: The prize honours research that reshaped how central banks and governments respond to booms, busts and shocks. Outlets framed it differently.

brief.what: Robert Hall (Stanford) and Michael Woodford (Columbia) won the 2026 Nobel memorial prize in economics for research on stabilising economies.
brief.who: The two laureates; the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. Economists Olivier Blanchard and John Cochrane commented.
brief.context: Their work underpins how central banks use interest rates and expectations to smooth booms and busts. Woodford's New Keynesian framework is the standard model in central banking.
brief.why: The committee said their work "generated a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy". Coverage differed: Nature stressed its influence on crisis policy, the Washington Examiner that their models have challenged recent Fed policy.
brief.next: They share about $1.2 million; the prize is presented in December.

also.author: Molly Parks
also.title: Two Americans win Nobel for economic model challenging government response to 2020s economic shocks
also.note: Frames the work as challenging recent Federal Reserve policy.

items.title: Trump announces Russian diesel deal amid soaring US fuel prices
items.author: Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and Reuters
items.summary: After a call with Putin, Trump said Russia will supply diesel to US and world markets, with prices up about 70% since the Iran war began. Coverage split sharply.

brief.what: President Trump said Russia agreed to supply diesel to the US and world markets after a call with Vladimir Putin.
brief.who: Trump; Putin; Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev; Senate Republicans including Thom Tillis, who oppose the deal.
brief.context: US diesel prices are near record highs (about $6.27 a gallon), up roughly 70% since the Iran war began. The G7 had just agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel.
brief.why: The administration wants lower fuel prices before the 3 November midterms. Trump's stated volumes (300,000 tons now, then more) don't add up to the total he gave.
brief.next: Critics question whether buying Russian fuel is legal under sanctions. Fox Business led with Trump's account; The Dispatch asked if the deal is legal.

also.author: Brie Stimson
also.title: Trump says Russia has agreed to deliver millions in diesel fuel after 'highly successful discussion'
also.note: Leads with Trump's account and the benefit to farmers and truckers.

also.author: Surya Gowda, Evan Spear, James P. Sutton, Ross Anderson
also.title: Is Trump's Diesel Deal Legal?

items.title: Rising fuel costs slash Delta's profit outlook despite strong demand
items.author: Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters
items.summary: Delta cut its 2026 earnings guidance as its fuel bill heads $6bn higher, even with fares up about 20% and premium revenue rising.

brief.what: Delta Air Lines cut its 2026 profit forecast because fuel costs will rise by about $6 billion this year, even though demand is strong.
brief.who: Delta and CEO Ed Bastian; analysts surveyed by LSEG; United Airlines, which reports next.
brief.context: US airlines spent nearly $43 billion on fuel in the first eight months, $13.2 billion more than a year earlier. Delta owns a refinery, which softens the blow.
brief.why: Jet fuel prices rose with the Iran war. Delta raised fares about 20% but not enough to offset fuel.
brief.next: Guidance is now $5.10-$5.60 a share (was $6.50-$7.50). United reports on 20 October.

items.title: White House sets up panel to review Fed Governor Lisa Cook's removal
items.author: Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters
items.summary: A three-member committee will decide whether there is cause to fire Cook over mortgage-document allegations, with a hearing on 5 November.

brief.what: The White House set up a three-member panel to decide whether Fed Governor Lisa Cook can be fired over alleged false statements on mortgage documents.
brief.who: Lisa Cook; President Trump; FHFA director Bill Pulte, who made the allegations; the Supreme Court.
brief.context: Trump first tried to fire Cook in August 2025; a judge blocked it, and the Supreme Court ruled a governor can only be removed for cause through a clear process.
brief.why: The case tests whether the president can pressure the Fed, which just raised interest rates for the first time in three years.
brief.next: Cook must attend a hearing on 5 November. Her term runs to 2038.

items.title: US suspends Microsoft and Adobe from visa programme amid fraud claims
items.author: Al Jazeera Staff, AP and Reuters
items.summary: The government suspended several tech firms from a skilled-worker green card route, citing $22bn in alleged visa fraud.

brief.what: The US suspended Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services from a programme that gives skilled foreign workers a path to permanent residency, citing fraud.
brief.who: The White House and VP JD Vance; Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling; Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, TCS; nine universities including Harvard and Stanford.
brief.context: The H-1B visa system is mostly used by tech firms, and nearly three-quarters of approvals go to Indian workers.
brief.why: The administration says employers are replacing Americans; it cites $22 billion in alleged visa fraud. Microsoft says 80% of its visas were for existing staff.
brief.next: A separate probe targets universities over J-1 visas.

items.title: US proposes $100,000 charge for international students to work after graduating
items.author: Dan Garisto
items.summary: A proposed rule would put a $100,000 price on OPT, the main route for foreign graduates to work in the US. Economists warn of a big drop in enrolment.

brief.what: The Department of Homeland Security proposed a $100,000 charge for international students to work in the US after graduation through OPT.
brief.who: DHS; universities; international students; economists Michael Clemens and Ina Ganguli.
brief.context: About a third of the US's 1.2 million international students used OPT in 2025-26. A $100,000 H-1B fee introduced in 2025 cut applications by a reported 90%.
brief.why: DHS says the rule would "combat fraud" and "protect US workers".
brief.next: It's a proposal; no final date. DHS projects enrolment could fall up to 44%, and Clemens estimates colleges could lose $2.5-4.2 billion a year.

items.title: Trucking firms file for bankruptcy as diesel costs keep surging
items.author: Sophia Compton
items.summary: At least eight transport companies filed for Chapter 11 in September as fuel and insurance costs rose.

brief.what: At least eight US transport companies filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September.
brief.who: Truckload LLC, Globemaster, Pacer Transport, Mill Creek Logistics and others; the White House.
brief.context: Diesel recently sold for about $6.26 a gallon at a Texas truck stop.
brief.why: Higher fuel and insurance costs; one owner said insurance was the bigger pressure.
brief.next: The administration temporarily allowed cheaper off-road diesel on highways, which could save 50 cents to $1 a gallon. Freight costs feed into prices across the economy.

items.title: IMF: UK to have second-highest inflation in the G7
items.author: Maurício Alencar
items.summary: The IMF expects UK inflation to average 3.3% this year, above target for a seventh year, with only the US higher.

brief.what: The IMF expects the UK to have the second-highest inflation in the G7 over the next two years.
brief.who: The IMF; Chancellor John Healey; Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey.
brief.context: Forecast: 3.3% inflation in 2026 and 2.8% in 2027, above the 2% target for a seventh year. Growth: 1.3% this year, 1.2% next.
brief.why: The IMF links price pressure to AI-driven investment and to wars squeezing oil and gas supply.
brief.next: Its forecasts assume Hormuz shipping resumes in March 2027. UK monetary policy is expected to stay tighter than elsewhere.

items.title: BP braces for up to $4.5bn hit as it pivots away from green energy
items.author: Samuel Norman
items.summary: BP will book a $3bn-$4.5bn impairment, mostly on its low-carbon businesses, after cutting transition spending.

brief.what: BP will book a $3 billion to $4.5 billion write-down in its third-quarter results, mostly on its low-carbon businesses.
brief.who: BP and new CEO Meg O'Neill; activist investor Elliott Management (over 5% of shares).
brief.context: BP has cut planned green spending by more than $5 billion a year, to a $2 billion ceiling, and sold most of its clean-energy venture portfolio.
brief.why: BP is pivoting back toward oil and gas under investor pressure, so green assets are now valued lower.
brief.next: O'Neill presents her first strategy update in New York in December. Net debt is expected to fall to $13.5-14.5 billion.

items.title: Tracking the negotiating texts at the COP17 biodiversity summit
items.author: Giuliana Viglione, Ho Woo Nam
items.summary: 196 parties meet in Yerevan from 19 to 30 October; countries are off track on 22 of 23 global nature targets, and finance is the main fight.

brief.what: Carbon Brief launched a tracker of the draft texts governments will negotiate at COP17, the UN biodiversity summit.
brief.who: 196 parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity; global south and global north country blocs.
brief.context: COP17 is halfway to the 2030 Kunming-Montreal targets, and countries are "not on track" for 22 of the 23 targets, according to the convention.
brief.why: Money is the main dispute: poorer countries want a new fund under the convention, richer ones prefer the existing Global Environment Facility. The same fight suspended COP16 in 2024.
brief.next: The summit runs in Yerevan, Armenia, from 19 to 30 October.

items.title: The race for lithium is becoming a race for water
items.author: Johanna Hansel, Carla Samon Ros, Wyatt Myskow
items.summary: Lithium projects near California's Salton Sea could need up to 100,000 acre-feet of water a year in a region facing Colorado River cuts.

brief.what: A lithium boom near California's Salton Sea is creating a fight over scarce water.
brief.who: Lithium developers including Hell's Kitchen (CEO Rod Colwell); Imperial County officials; the Imperial Irrigation District; local residents.
brief.context: Companies want to extract lithium for batteries from underground brine. The county projects up to 100,000 acre-feet of water a year for full buildout.
brief.why: EV battery demand drives the boom, but the region must also cut water use by 250,000 acre-feet from 2027 under Colorado River limits.
brief.next: An appeals court ruled against Hell's Kitchen's approval over water supply; the legal fight continues.

items.title: How a bid to beat drought drove Corpus Christi to the brink
items.author: Dylan Baddour, Neena Satija
items.summary: Corpus Christi spent at least $50m on a desalination plant that was never built, as costs rose from $140m to $1.2bn.

brief.what: Corpus Christi, Texas, has spent at least $50 million on a seawater desalination plant that was never built.
brief.who: City leaders; industrial water users OxyChem, Valero and Citgo; community organiser Isabel Araiza; Governor Greg Abbott.
brief.context: The plan, approved in 2018, exempted big industrial users from drought surcharges in return for funding.
brief.why: Costs rose from $140 million to $1.2 billion, and the city fired its contractor. Reservoirs nearly ran dry this spring.
brief.next: Voters decide on the industry exemption in November. Abandoning the plant could mean repaying $235 million in state loans plus interest.

items.title: Ex-OpenAI researchers say they were fired for raising safety concerns
items.author: John Power
items.summary: Three researchers say they were dismissed over safety work; OpenAI says it was misconduct involving company information.

brief.what: Three former OpenAI safety researchers say they were fired for their safety work.
brief.who: Researchers Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang; OpenAI.
brief.context: The AI industry is debating how to control powerful models. Last month six companies signed a voluntary safety accord that critics called nonbinding.
brief.why: OpenAI says they were dismissed for mishandling company information; the researchers deny that and say they were doing their jobs.
brief.next: Their open letter warns of a "chilling" effect on staff who raise concerns.

items.title: Plague scare: what scientists know, and what Russia won't say
items.author: Max Kozlov
items.summary: A researcher died at a Siberian plague lab, possibly of pneumonic plague. Experts say the outbreak risk is low but surveillance gaps are real.

brief.what: A 28-year-old researcher died at a plague research lab in Irkutsk, Siberia, possibly of pneumonic plague.
brief.who: Russia's health regulator; the WHO and the US government; biosecurity expert Gregory Koblentz.
brief.context: About 200 people may have been exposed and quarantined. Russia says tests found no dangerous pathogens.
brief.why: The cause hasn't been confirmed; Russia called it pneumonia of "unknown" origin.
brief.next: The WHO and US want epidemiological data. Experts say a wider outbreak is unlikely because plague is treatable.

items.title: IMF warns AI is a 'slow-moving tsunami' that could hit 60% of jobs in rich economies
items.author: Saskia Koopman
items.summary: IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva says AI could affect 40% of jobs worldwide, with young workers most exposed.

brief.what: IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva warned that AI could affect 40% of jobs worldwide and 60% in advanced economies.
brief.who: The IMF; Georgieva; UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan.
brief.context: An IMF study found 10% of US jobs now need advanced AI skills. An OECD report says nearly four in five London jobs are highly exposed to generative AI.
brief.why: AI is automating routine entry-level work that used to start professional careers.
brief.next: Georgieva urged investment in lifelong learning and asked how governments will tax income that shifts from workers to capital.

items.title: Supreme Court case tests how much judges must defer to federal agencies
items.author: Damon Root
items.summary: Beaird v. United States asks whether courts must follow the Sentencing Commission's commentary, reviving a wider debate about the administrative state.

brief.what: The Supreme Court will hear Beaird v. United States on how much judges must defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary.
brief.who: Kendrick Beaird (defendant); the US government; the Sentencing Commission; Justices Kagan and Gorsuch, whose past opinions frame the debate.
brief.context: Beaird's sentence was raised because his magazine held 17 rounds; the commission's commentary, not the guideline itself, defines "large-capacity" as over 15.
brief.why: Reason's Damon Root argues it revives a wider fight over courts deferring to federal agencies ("the administrative state"). That's the author's view.
brief.next: Oral arguments come first; a decision is expected later in the term.

items.title: Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in immigration fraud probe
items.author: Tosin Akintola
items.summary: A court-authorised search tied to Omar's immigration paperwork; she calls it an abuse of power, the administration says it's not political.

brief.what: Federal investigators searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home under a court-authorised warrant.
brief.who: Rep. Omar; Homeland Security Investigations; DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin; VP JD Vance.
brief.context: CBS reports the probe centres on Omar's immigration paperwork; the NYT reports possible false-statement and document-fraud offences.
brief.why: Officials say it's a criminal investigation and "not political"; Omar calls it an "outrageous abuse of power". Reason's author argues it is likely politically driven.
brief.next: No charges have been filed.

items.title: Wall Street finishes a record-setting week with gains
items.author: Stan Choe
items.summary: The S&P 500 closed at 7,811 after a week of records, even as the 10-year Treasury yield sits near its highest since 2002 and Brent oil above $100.

brief.what: US stocks ended a week of record highs with gains: the S&P 500 rose 0.6% to 7,811.54, the Dow 0.8% to 51,654.95 and the Nasdaq 0.6%.
brief.who: Investors; telecom stocks (T-Mobile -13%, AT&T -10%, Verizon -9%); tower owners (Crown Castle +16%, American Tower +9%); SpaceX; Humana (+12%).
brief.context: The 10-year Treasury yield is 5.24%, near its highest since 2002, and Brent crude is $104.72. Michigan consumers now expect 4.7% inflation, up from 3.4% before the Iran war.
brief.why: Strong profit expectations are lifting stocks. SpaceX's purchase of mobile spectrum sank wireless carriers and lifted tower stocks; yields rose on inflation and US debt worries.
brief.next: Big banks (Citigroup, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo) report earnings next, starting earnings season.

items.title: Stocks slip as the 30-year Treasury yield hits a 24-year high
items.author: Stephen Culp
items.summary: Brent briefly topped $100 and long-term borrowing costs jumped, reviving worries that the Fed will keep raising rates.

brief.what: US stocks closed slightly lower (S&P 500 -0.2%, Dow -0.7%) as Brent crude briefly rose above $100 and the 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest in 24 years.
brief.who: Investors; the Federal Reserve; the International Energy Agency; portfolio manager Thomas Martin of GLOBALT.
brief.context: In September the Fed raised rates for the first time since July 2023. Markets now see under a 20% chance of another hike in October, down from 37.6% a week earlier.
brief.why: Iran-war oil supply fears revived inflation worries, and heavy government and corporate debt drove a global bond sell-off. Martin said investors were taking profits after a correction "didn't happen".
brief.next: Stocks pared losses after the IEA agreed to speed up oil stock releases. Earnings season starts next week; analysts expect 30.6% S&P 500 profit growth.

items.title: MLB's salary cap fight is about labour costs, not competitive balance, argues Reason
items.author: Jason Russell
items.summary: An opinion column argues baseball owners want a salary cap to hold down player pay, and expects a lockout.

brief.what: Reason's managing editor argues Major League Baseball owners want a salary cap mainly to limit what they pay players, not to make the league more balanced.
brief.who: MLB team owners (pushing for a cap); the players' union (resisting); President Trump (backing the owners); the National Labor Relations Board.
brief.context: Small-market teams such as Milwaukee (19th in payroll), Tampa Bay (28th) and Cleveland (30th) already compete, which the author says weakens the balance argument. Caps in other sports have had scandals.
brief.why: In the author's view, owners are "almost certainly focused on keeping down their labor costs". He cites studies suggesting caps don't create balance. This is an opinion piece.
brief.next: The author expects a lockout. Owners plan to offer a salary floor, which the union is unlikely to accept.

items.title: The Rugby League World Cup starts this week behind a paywall, and that's a problem, says City AM
items.author: Simon Dent
items.summary: Every match is exclusive to Premier Sports in the UK and Ireland, after the BBC showed them all in 2022. The author says that limits new fans.

brief.what: The 2026 Rugby League World Cup starts this week, with every match shown only on pay-TV channel Premier Sports in Britain and Ireland.
brief.who: Premier Sports (exclusive broadcaster); the BBC (which showed every match in 2022); author Simon Dent, an entrepreneur; teams including Australia, New Zealand, Samoa, Tonga and England.
brief.context: The 2022 tournament on free TV drew many first-time viewers. Australia remain the team to beat, and Samoa reached the last final.
brief.why: The author argues a paywall cuts the chance of new people discovering the sport, though he accepts the deal may make commercial sense. This is an opinion piece.
brief.next: He calls for podcasts, documentaries and creator collaborations to market the sport beyond existing fans.

items.title: Award-winning microscopy video disqualified over AI use
items.author: Rachel Fieldhouse
items.summary: Nikon stripped the winner of its Small World in Motion contest after scientists questioned whether AI had been used to make the video.

brief.what: Nikon disqualified the first-place entry in its Small World in Motion microscopy video competition because it broke rules banning AI-generated videos.
brief.who: Ning Xu, an optical engineer now at the National University of Singapore (entrant); Nikon Instruments (organiser); scientists on LinkedIn who flagged the video.
brief.context: The video of moving lung cilia won on 15 September. Xu said an AI model was used in post-processing to enhance parts of the image.
brief.why: Scientists said some features looked biologically implausible. Nikon said the decision rested "solely" on eligibility and is not a judgment of Xu's reputation or intent.
brief.next: No further steps were reported. Xu did not respond to Nature's request for comment.

week.text: The fuel shock is spreading. US diesel is up about 70% since the Iran war began; Trump announced a contested Russian diesel deal, Delta cut its profit forecast, and small trucking firms are going bankrupt.
Stocks hit records even as borrowing costs climb: the S&P 500 closed at 7,811 while the 10-year Treasury yield sits near its highest since 2002 and Brent oil is above $100.
Aerospace: Airbus passed 1,100 net orders for the year, Biman Bangladesh placed its first Airbus order, JetBlue won Spirit's LaGuardia slots, and Joby lost a $116.9m trade-secret verdict.
Central bank independence is being tested: a White House panel will decide whether Fed Governor Lisa Cook can be removed, with a hearing on 5 November.
The US is tightening skilled-worker routes: Microsoft, Adobe and others were suspended from a green card programme, and a $100,000 fee was proposed for foreign graduates' work permits.
